 Student Loan Debt Drags on Retirement Savings; What Feds With Debt Can Do
 Published: November 11, 2026 
More in: Retirement & Financial Planning Report 
 While the TSP has not announced it offers the SECURE 2.0 loan match, there are some things federal employees with loans can do to get a leg up. Image: Vitalii Vodolazskyi/Shutterstock.com 
 By: FEDweek Staff Federal employees paying off student loans may be falling behind on retirement savings – and at the same time missing out on government matching. A study by the Employee Benefit Research Institute shows that student loan debt – unsurprisingly – leads to less saving, lower rates of contribution and smaller retirement balances than debt-free peers, and that gap remains long into their careers.
 “Among 401(k) plan participants in their 40s, those with student loan debt had median retirement account balances approximately 45% lower than participants without student loan debt,” it said, adding that “While student loan debt is most prevalent among younger workers, the research found student loan debt among participants across age, income, tenure and retirement account balance levels.”
 While the study did not break out patterns in the federal TSP program, that program is comparable to 401(k) plans in general. And it points to similar choices federal workers face: whether to put extra money toward loans or the TSP, and if they are capturing the full agency match (by contributing at least five percent).
 It said that among those with such plans, between ages 25 and 69, 38 percent of those age 25-29 have student loan debt, compared for example with 21 percent of those age 40-44 and 13 percent of those age 55-59. Among the youngest group, 76 percent of those with student debt and who access to such a plan were investing in it, compared with 84 percent of those without such debt.
 Student loan debt also affects the amounts that those with such debt invest, if they do so at all. Those with student loan debt generally did so at lower rates—as much as 15 percent lower for those age 50-54, who are running short on years to build up their retirement savings before retiring.
 “The retirement savings gap persisted over time. Longitudinal analysis found that participants with student loan debt continued to have lower contribution rates and account balances. Despite some narrowing of the gap, older participants with student loan debt continued to have account balances approximately 30% lower than participants without student loan debt,” it said.
 One reason, it added, is that by investing at lower levels, those with student debt are giving up some of the employer matching contributions available to them. While those matching formulas vary among plans, across all 401(k) investors, 39 percent invested less than 4 percent of income, 50 percent less than 5 percent and 61 percent less than 6 percent.
 The EBRI study’s focus was a provision in the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 that allows employers to make matching retirement contributions based on an employee’s qualified student loan payments, even if the employee isn’t contributing to the plan. EBRI estimated that universal adoption could add $11.2 billion a year in matching contributions under a 4 percent maximum match, or $20.2 billion under a 6 percent maximum.
 While the TSP has not announced it offers the SECURE 2.0 loan match, there are some things federal employees with loans can do to get a leg up:
 Make sure you are contributing at least five percent to get the full government match.
 Ask about agency loan repayment programs. For example, agencies may repay up to $10,000 a year – up to $60,000 total – in exchange for a three year service agreement.
 Check out Public Service Loan Forgiveness. Federal employment qualifies for PSLF, which forgives remaining federal Direct Loan balances tax-free after 120 qualifying payments. (You may be able to combine different education loans into a direct loan.) New Education Department rules took effect July 1, 2026, including a new Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) that counts toward PSLF. Check their status and certify employment at StudentAid.gov/pslf.
